newsitem.title: USA: Citadel officials faulted on integration - report.
newsitem.headline: Citadel officials faulted on integration - report.

text.p: A report released on Tuesday faulted officials at The Citadel for their handling of the integration of women and recommended the formerly all-male military college hire more female officers.

The report, by a committee comprised of former Citadel officials, community leaders and a female graduate of the U.S. Air Force Academy, said The Citadel's leaders had failed to develop and communicate a plan for assimilating women.

It made 13 recommendations, including hiring more female officers and further integrating barracks and evaluating the school's fourth-class system, an aggressive style of training new cadets to be leaders.
"Unfortunately the image of the Corps has been tarnished in recent months by the unacceptable actions of a relatively few cadets and the practices of some in authority," it said.

"Strong leadership measures must be taken at every level to assist the Corps to regain the credibility, the prestige and the reputation it deserves well beyond the confines of The Citadel campus," the report said.
Two of the four women who enrolled in the publicly supported military college last fall dropped out this year, saying they had been hazed and harassed.
Federal and state agencies were investigating the allegations by Kim Messer and Jeanie Mentavlos. The other two women have reported no harassment.

In its two-month review, the committee interviewed 23 Citadel officials and cadets. The committee found fault with the Board of Visitors, the school's governing body, for not developing a vision for assimilating woman into the corps that was broadcast loudly to all who would listen.

"The committee is convinced that many quarters of the college do not fully comprehend the implications with attendant responsibilities that The Citadel is now a co-educational military college," the report said.
The committee suggested that small groups of cadets be "indoctrinated" in methods of bringing women fully into the life of the college.

It also said the public relations department had projected the image that the school was resisting having women in the Corps. An aggressive public relations effort should be launched to tell the country, not just the news media, that this idea is no longer so, the report said.
